article: Why do poached and scrambled egg entries show different protein per gram?
Compare the cooked USDA entries and check which ingredients your log already includes.
USDA SR Legacy whole cooked poached and scrambled egg entries. These are independent preparations.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: The poached egg reference lists 12.51 g protein per 100 g. Scrambled egg lists 9.99 g. If the eggs you cooked came from the same carton, that database contrast cannot tell you how much protein disappeared. The entries describe finished preparations, which can have different yields and ingredients.
Select the reference for the finished dish

At an 80 g cooked weight, the two rows give 10.0 and 8.0 g protein respectively. Use the same basis for both, especially if one logged item already represents a finished dish. Add milk or butter separately only when the entry excludes those ingredients.
Record a homemade scratch recipe from its actual ingredients if the finished database description is unclear.

article: Does tahini add as much protein as peanut butter to a sauce?
Compare two 16 g weighed spoonfuls and see how doubling the tahini changes the answer.
USDA SR Legacy roasted-toasted-kernel tahini and smooth peanut butter without salt.
copy: A 16 g spoonful of roasted-kernel tahini gives about 2.7 g protein, compared with about 3.6 g from the same weight of smooth unsalted peanut butter. Their calories are close at these portions. Doubling the tahini gives 5.4 g protein from the paste and also doubles the calories.
Separate the paste from the rest of the recipe

Measure the paste before thinning it. Water changes the sauce’s weight, while a flavored liquid or sweetener can contribute its own nutrients. If the finished recipe is split into two equal servings, take half the paste contribution for each.
Use the plain product reference or package label for the exact paste. Avoid treating a finished dressing as undiluted tahini.

article: Does toasted rye have more fiber and less sodium than white toast?
Compare two 35 g toasted portions with the actual sodium and fiber fields shown side by side.
USDA SR Legacy toasted rye and toasted commercial white bread. Equal finished toasted weight.
copy: For 35 g of each toasted bread, rye gives about 2.2 g fiber and 232 mg sodium. The white toast example gives about 1.0 g fiber and 188 mg sodium. In this pair, more fiber comes with more sodium rather than less.
Match the listed bread and toasted weight

The USDA figures describe two named breads after toasting, which can change their weight. If you are logging a packaged slice, its label usually describes the way it comes from the package. Apply that label to the labeled slice amount before adding butter or another spread.
The outcome may change for low-sodium rye or a different white bread. Compare their actual labels if you have both packages.

article: Will a pinto-to-black-bean swap substantially change fiber in a chili?
Compare a 400 g cooked bean base and calculate two four-serving recipes.
USDA SR Legacy pinto and black beans, both boiled without salt. Bean-only contribution.
copy: In a four-serving chili, 400 g cooked pinto beans contributes 36 g fiber from the beans. At the same cooked weight, black beans provide 34.8 g. That works out to a difference of about 0.3 g per serving, before the rest of the pot is counted.
Hold the total bean weight constant

Protein is also close in these unsalted USDA entries. The swap changes the whole batch by only about 0.6 g of protein. If you use a canned product, choose the right basis for the weighed amount and whether you discard the liquid.
For the complete chili, add the tomatoes, meat, vegetables or other ingredients separately and divide the finished portions by weight or by equal servings.

article: Does pearled barley give more fiber than millet after cooking?
Match a cooked bowl and see how the protein and fiber comparisons diverge.
USDA SR Legacy cooked millet and cooked pearled barley. Example uses 175 g cooked portions.
copy: Cooked pearled barley supplies about 6.7 g fiber in a 175 g bowl. The cooked millet reference supplies about 2.3 g. Millet gives about 6.1 g protein at that weight, compared with about 4.0 g for the barley. The ranking changes when you switch nutrients.
Keep the grain preparation in the record

A half-and-half base made with 87.5 g of each provides about 4.5 g fiber. The figures compare prepared weights and exclude broth, oil, seasonings and toppings. Barley is a different grain from millet and is not a suitable substitution for someone who needs to avoid gluten.
Use the label for prepared grain blends and identify the grain and cooking basis before using a generic food record.
table: Protein and fiber in equal cooked bowls

article: What does the bread contribute in a pita versus two corn tortillas?
Compare an example pita and two corn tortillas before fillings are added.
USDA SR Legacy whole-wheat pita and ordinary ready-to-bake-or-fry corn tortillas. Example weights identify the base only.
copy: A 60 g whole-wheat pita contributes about 157 kcal and 5.9 g protein in the USDA entry. Two 25 g corn tortillas together contribute about 109 kcal and 2.9 g protein. These are the bases before fillings, oil or cooking additions.
A piece count needs an edible weight

If your tortillas weigh 35 g each, their combined 70 g contributes about 153 kcal. The difference in energy is then only a few calories. For a product that gives a labeled value per tortilla, count the pieces according to that label rather than assuming a standard weight.
Use a separate entry for fried shells or wraps that include other ingredients. Their preparation can change the comparison.

article: Does breaded seafood carry the same protein as plain crab meat?
Compare a weighed serving of fried breaded scallops and cooked blue crab, keeping the preparations visible.
USDA SR Legacy blue crab cooked with moist heat and mixed-species scallops breaded and fried. Independent seafood types and recipes.
copy: In these USDA entries, 100 g of cooked blue crab and 100 g of fried breaded scallops each have about 18 g protein. The scallop preparation lists 216 kcal per 100 g, compared with 83 kcal in the cooked crab. Similar protein does not make these portions nutritionally equivalent.
Read protein alongside the finished preparation

For an 85 g portion, those values scale to about 15.2 and 15.4 g protein respectively. The comparison changes both the seafood and its preparation. It cannot isolate the calories added by breading alone or predict an individual restaurant recipe.
Use the finished breaded record for a finished breaded serving. Add dipping sauce separately when it is not included in the label.

article: How does roasted duck meat compare with roasted dark chicken meat?
Use meat-only servings to compare the protein and total fat of roasted poultry.
USDA SR Legacy domestic duck meat only and broiler dark chicken meat only, roasted.
copy: A 100 g cooked portion of domestic duck meat has about 23.5 g protein and 11.2 g fat in the USDA entry. Its 100 g dark chicken counterpart gives about 27.4 g protein and 9.7 g fat. Both records leave the skin out.
The edible meat is the comparison

If the dark chicken portion is 85 g, it comes close to matching the protein of 100 g duck, at about 23.3 g. The remaining differences come from the references and serving sizes. A crispy skin portion or glaze needs its own nutrients, especially when comparing a finished restaurant dish.
Identify the cut and keep the cooked edible weight with the entry. The table excludes bones and anything left on the plate.
table: Protein and fat in roasted meat without skin

article: What changes if ricotta replaces cream cheese on toast?
Compare equal-weight spreads before adding bread, fruit or seasoning.
USDA SR Legacy whole-milk ricotta and cream cheese at 30 g each. Independent reference foods.
copy: A 30 g layer of USDA whole-milk ricotta gives about 45 kcal and 2.3 g protein. The same weight of cream cheese gives 105 kcal and about 1.8 g protein. Most of the energy difference here comes with a large difference in the fat values.
Use a fixed weight for the spread

If you use 60 g ricotta, the estimate is about 90 kcal and 4.5 g protein. That amount remains slightly below the energy of the 30 g cream cheese example. The result does not cover flavored tubs, whipped products or fat-reduced versions.
Add the toast separately when logging the finished breakfast. The examples compare only the spread.

article: Does 20 g of protein take the same amount of firm and soft tofu?
Compare two calcium-and-nigari tofu references and calculate the portions that would tie.
USDA SR Legacy firm and soft tofu, both prepared with calcium sulfate and magnesium chloride.
copy: The two USDA calcium-and-nigari tofu records have 9.04 g protein per 100 g for firm tofu and 7.17 g for soft tofu. You would need about 221 g of the firm entry or 279 g of the soft entry to supply 20 g protein mathematically.
Firmness does not replace the actual label

At 150 g each, the two estimates are 13.6 and 10.8 g. Some firm tofu products have much greater concentrations than the USDA firm example here. Check the label for your product rather than assuming the word firm identifies a single value.
Weigh the portion using the same preparation the source describes. A fried or baked item can differ after moisture loss and other changes.
table: Matching a hypothetical 20 g protein amount

article: Does a low-sodium can of black beans match home-cooked black beans for fiber?
Read two USDA references by edible serving, keeping sodium and fiber separate.
USDA SR Legacy boiled unsalted black beans and a low-sodium canned black bean record. Independent references.
copy: The USDA low-sodium canned reference provides 6.9 g fiber per 100 g. The boiled unsalted reference provides 8.7 g. At 120 g, that is about 8.3 g versus 10.4 g. Both records describe black beans, but the reference forms are different.
The front-of-pack sodium claim does not settle fiber

The canned row also has 138 mg sodium per 100 g, while the boiled unsalted row has 1 mg. The figures do not isolate the effect of canning or predict what rinsing does to the product in your kitchen. Check whether a particular label’s serving includes packing liquid.
Record the measured solids using a matching entry whenever you can. If you use the liquid, keep the source scope visible.
table: USDA black bean references at 120 g

article: When two Alaska pollock entries disagree, which one belongs in your fish comparison?
Compare two published pollock records and see how the choice changes a 120 g estimate.
USDA SR Legacy Alaska pollock cooked dry heat may contain additives, a separate Alaska pollock cooked record and dry-heat tilapia.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: USDA has two cooked Alaska pollock entries with different protein values. One lists 23.48 g per 100 g and specifies dry heat with possible moisture-retaining additives. Another lists 19.42 g. Both use 100 g, but the descriptions and nutrient records differ.
Keep the complete food description

At 120 g fish, the estimates are about 28.2 and 23.3 g. A dry-heat tilapia reference at the same amount is about 31.4 g. Use the best match for the actual fish and preparation. The records do not tell you how much of the gap came from a single production step.
If a product label gives data for your exact fillet, use it instead of averaging unrelated reference records.

article: Can replacing half the pecans with almonds change a snack’s protein much?
Compare equal nut portions and calculate a half-and-half snack using two USDA entries.
USDA SR Legacy almonds and pecans, plain edible kernels. Equal mixture by weight.
copy: Thirty grams of almonds provides about 6.3 g protein in the USDA reference. The same weight of pecans provides around 2.8 g. Splitting the portion evenly gives about 4.5 g protein, roughly 1.8 g more than the all-pecan portion.
Change the ratio without changing snack weight

The fiber moves by less than a gram in this example. Fifteen grams of almonds gives 1.875 g fiber and 15 g pecans gives 1.44 g. Adding those unrounded numbers gives about 3.3 g. Treat a nut and dried-fruit blend as a different recipe if the label already reports the whole mixture.
Use the weight of edible kernels. Roughly equal handfuls can give an unequal mixture.

article: How much fiber changes when you replace half the pasta with bulgur?
Build two bowls at the same cooked weight using USDA enriched pasta and cooked bulgur.
USDA SR Legacy enriched pasta cooked without added salt and cooked bulgur. Plain bases only.
copy: A 180 g portion of plain cooked enriched pasta gives about 3.2 g fiber and 10.4 g protein. Replacing half its cooked weight with bulgur raises fiber to about 5.7 g and lowers protein to about 8.0 g in these USDA entries.
Hold the cooked bowl weight fixed

This uses 90 g of each prepared food. There is no need to estimate how much dry food each one started with when both weights were measured after cooking. A sauced dish would add its own values. Bulgur is wheat, so the swap does not create a gluten-free meal.
If you prefer to compare dry products, use dry entries for both and keep that separate from the finished-bowl comparison.

article: Is the breaded shrimp entry always higher in sodium?
Compare two USDA shrimp records and see why an unbreaded preparation can still list more sodium.
USDA SR Legacy mixed-species shrimp cooked breaded and fried versus moist heat, which may contain additives to retain moisture.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: The USDA mixed-shrimp reference cooked with moist heat lists 947 mg sodium per 100 g and notes that it can include moisture-retaining additives. Its breaded and fried reference lists 344 mg sodium for the same weight. The directions differ for sodium and calories.
Read the source description before using the row

The two entries are independent foods. Do not subtract them to estimate the effect of adding breading to the same shrimp. At 85 g cooked, the two sodium values scale to about 805 and 292 mg respectively. A matching package declaration can give a better estimate for a specific purchase.
Keep cooking style and ingredients with the portion. This comparison excludes sauces and added seasoning after cooking.
